hints: Think about what happens when a carbonate decomposes and which ion is responsible for breaking up the $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ ion.
Compare the $\text{M}^{2+}$ ions down Group 2 from $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ to $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ in terms of size when the charge stays the same.
Link the distorting power of the cation to how easily the $\text{C-O}$ bond in carbonate can break to form $\text{CO}_2$.
walkthrough:
Picture what thermal decomposition means**
You are heating $\text{MCO}_3(s)$ to give $\text{MO}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)$. Think of the $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ ion as needing to break apart into $\text{O}^{2-}$ and $\text{CO}_2$. Anything that pulls electron density away from the carbonate and distorts it will help that break happen at a lower temperature.

Compare the cations down the group**
All the ions are $2+$, so charge is constant. What changes is size. $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is very small, $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ is larger, $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ larger still, $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ largest. Smaller means the same $2+$ charge is packed into a smaller volume, so charge density is higher at the top of the group.

Link charge density to polarising power**
A small, highly charging $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ pulls hard on the electron cloud of the neighbouring $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ ion. This polarisation distorts the carbonate, weakens a $\text{C-O}$ bond and effectively pre-breaks it toward $\text{CO}_2$. A large $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ has low charge density, polarises very little, so the carbonate stays intact to a much higher temperature. That is why stability increases down the group.

Final answer: Thermal stability increases down Group 2.
Down the group the radius of $\text{M}^{2+}$ increases, so charge density decreases.
The smaller cation at the top more strongly polarises / distorts the $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ ion, weakening it and making decomposition easier.

hints: Compare $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ for the two factors that control polarising power: ionic charge and ionic size.
walkthrough:
Put the two cations side by side**
$\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is $2+$ and very small because it is in Period 3 with a high nuclear charge for its size. $\text{Na}^{+}$ is only $1+$ and is larger than $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ as it has less proton pull on the same electron shells. Lower charge spread over a larger ion means much lower charge density for $\text{Na}^{+}$. Lower charge density means much weaker distortion of the carbonate ion, so sodium carbonate needs far more heat to decompose. In fact it does not decompose on normal laboratory heating.

Final answer: $\text{Na}^{+}$ has a smaller ionic charge ($1+$ vs $2+$) and larger ionic radius than $\text{Mg}^{2+}$, so lower charge density and less polarisation of $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$, hence $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ is more stable to heat.

hints: Remember that two $\text{HCO}_3^{-}$ ions combine to give one carbonate, plus the two gases that come from $\text{H}$ and extra $\text{C}$ and $\text{O}$.
walkthrough:
Build the products logically**
Hydrogencarbonate decomposition always gives the solid metal carbonate plus carbon dioxide and water. You need two $\text{KHCO}_3$ to supply $\text{K}_2$ for $\text{K}_2\text{CO}_3$. Check atoms: left $2\text{K}$, $2\text{H}$, $2\text{C}$, $6\text{O}$. Right $\text{K}_2\text{CO}_3 + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$ gives $2\text{K}$, $2\text{H}$, $2\text{C}$, $6\text{O}$. Balanced.

hints: Apply the same polarisation idea as for carbonates, but now compare two Group 1 cations $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{K}^{+}$.
walkthrough:
Use size to predict ease of decomposition**
Both cations are $1+$, so only size matters. $\text{Na}^{+}$ is smaller than $\text{K}^{+}$, so it has the higher charge density and stronger polarising power toward the $\text{HCO}_3^{-}$ ion. That extra distortion makes $\text{NaHCO}_3$ break down more readily, so it decomposes at the lower temperature.
Final answer: $\text{NaHCO}_3$ decomposes at the lower temperature because $\text{Na}^{+}$ is smaller / has larger charge density than $\text{K}^{+}$, so greater polarisation.

hints: Start by sketching the Born-Haber cycle for $\text{K}_2\text{O}$ with $\Delta H_f$ at the bottom and gaseous ions $2\text{K}^{+}(g) + \text{O}^{2-}(g)$ at the top.
List what you need from the Data Booklet for potassium and oxygen that is not in the table: first ionisation energy of K and $\text{O=O}$ bond energy.
Remember the stoichiometry: you need $2$ moles of K atomisation and ionisation, and $1/2$ mole of $\text{O}_2$ dissociation for one mole of $\text{K}_2\text{O}$.
walkthrough:
Set up the Hess cycle relationship**
For the formation: $$2\text{K}(s) + \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{K}_2\text{O}(s)$$ The Born-Haber route goes up to ions then down via lattice formation: $$\Delta H_f = 2\Delta H_{at}[\text{K}(s)] + 2IE_1(\text{K}) + \frac{1}{2}D(\text{O=O}) + (EA_1 + EA_2) + \Delta H_{latt}$$ Rearranged: $$\Delta H_{latt} = \Delta H_f - 2(\Delta H_{at} + IE) - \frac{1}{2}D(\text{O=O}) - (EA_1 + EA_2)$$

Insert the numbers with correct multiples**
From the table: $\Delta H_{at} = +89 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, $EA_1 = -141 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, $EA_2 = +798 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, $\Delta H_f = -361 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. From the Data Booklet: $IE_1(\text{K}) = +418 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, $D(\text{O=O}) = +496 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. So: $$\Delta H_{latt} = -361 - 2(89) - 2(418) - 496/2 - (-141 + 798)$$

Calculate carefully**
$2(89) = 178$, $2(418) = 836$, $496/2 = 248$, $(-141+798) = +657$. Then: $$\Delta H_{latt} = -361 -178 -836 -248 -657 = -2280 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ The large negative value is expected for lattice formation from gaseous ions.

hints: Recall that lattice energy magnitude depends on ionic charge and on how closely the oppositely charged ions can approach each other.
walkthrough:
Compare ion packing**
Both oxides contain $\text{O}^{2-}$ with two $1+$ cations, so charge is identical. The difference is size: $\text{Na}^{+}$ is significantly smaller than $\text{K}^{+}$. Smaller ions get closer together, the electrostatic attraction $\propto q^+q^-/r$ is stronger, more energy is released when the lattice forms, so $\Delta H_{latt}$ is more exothermic, more negative, for $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$.

Final answer: Lattice energy of $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ is more negative than that of $\text{K}_2\text{O}$ because $\text{Na}^{+}$ is smaller / has larger charge density, so stronger attraction between ions / stronger ionic bonds.
